NON-DISPARAGEMENT AGREEMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

CALIFORNIA'S SETTLEMENT-AGREEMENT DISCLOSURE BAN (SEXUAL HARASSMENT, DISCRIMINATION, RETALIATION)
California law prohibits including, in a settlement agreement resolving a claim filed in a civil action or an administrative complaint, any provision that prevents or restricts disclosure of factual information related to a claim of: sexual assault; sexual harassment; workplace harassment or discrimination, an employer's failure to prevent it, or retaliation against a person for reporting or opposing it; or harassment, discrimination, or retaliation by the owner of a housing accommodation. A court also can't enter an order, by stipulation or otherwise, that restricts disclosure of that same information. For an agreement entered into on or after January 1, 2019, a provision that violates this rule is void as a matter of law and against public policy, not merely voidable or unenforceable by one side.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "a provision within a settlement agreement that prevents or restricts the disclosure of factual information related to a claim filed in a civil action or a complaint filed in an administrative action, regarding any of the following, is prohibited: (1) An act of sexual assault that is not governed by subdivision (a) of Section 1002. (2) An act of sexual harassment, as defined in Section 51.9 of the Civil Code. (3) An act of workplace harassment or discrimination, failure to prevent an act of workplace harassment or discrimination, or an act of retaliation against a person for reporting or opposing harassment or discrimination, as described in subdivisions (a), (h), (i), (j), and (k) of Section 12940 of the Government Code."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001(a) (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Confidential Settlement Agreements, covered claims and disclosure-restriction ban (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1001)
  "in a civil matter described in paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (a), a court shall not enter, by stipulation or otherwise, an order that restricts the disclosure of information in a manner that conflicts with subdivision (a). ... a provision within a settlement agreement that prevents or restricts the disclosure of factual information related to the claim described in subdivision (a) that is entered into on or after January 1, 2019, is void as a matter of law and against public policy."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001(b), (d) (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Confidential Settlement Agreements, court-order limit and void-as-a-matter-of-law rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1001)
  "A contract or proposed contract for the sale or lease of consumer goods or services may not include a provision waiving the consumer’s right to make any statement regarding the seller or lessor or its employees or agents, or concerning the goods or services."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1670.8(a)(1) (Leginfo text), California Civil Code, consumer-contract gag-clause ban — an unrelated statute, cited here only to correct a common misattribution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1670.8)
  Known gap: This statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001) applies specifically to a settlement agreement resolving a claim already filed in court or with an administrative agency — it is not a general rule for every severance or separation agreement, including one offered before any claim is filed. A separate, broader California statute reaches ordinary separation agreements themselves; it's covered in this document's next clauses. A correction to a common assumption: California Civil Code § 1670.8 is sometimes assumed to be the state's employment non-disparagement statute, but it is not — it's an unrelated consumer-protection statute that bars a contract for the sale or lease of consumer goods or services from waiving a consumer's right to make statements about the seller or the goods or services (commonly discussed as an anti-"gag clause" rule for online reviews). It has nothing to do with employment, severance, or settlement agreements; it is quoted below only to make this correction concrete and verifiable, not as authority for anything else in this document. Separately, this clause's description of the covered claim categories relies on § 1001(a)'s own cross-references to Civil Code § 51.9 (defining sexual harassment) and Government Code §§ 12940 and 12955 (defining the covered forms of discrimination, harassment, and retaliation); those cross-referenced definitions were not separately fetched or independently verified in this research — only § 1001's own text, which names them, was fetched and confirmed. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.

CARVE-OUTS: COMPENSATION CONFIDENTIALITY AND CLAIMANT IDENTITY
The same statute preserves two things a settlement agreement can still keep confidential even though the underlying facts of a covered claim can't be gagged. First, at the claimant's own request (not the other side's), the agreement may shield the claimant's identity and any facts that would reveal it, including court pleadings — unless a government agency or public official is a party to the settlement, in which case this identity-shielding option isn't available. Second, and separately, the statute doesn't prohibit a provision that keeps confidential the amount paid in settlement of the claim — the dollar figure can still be kept confidential even where the facts underlying the claim cannot.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "a provision that shields the identity of the claimant and all facts that could lead to the discovery of the claimant’s identity, including pleadings filed in court, may be included within a settlement agreement at the request of the claimant. This subdivision does not apply if a government agency or public official is a party to the settlement agreement."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001(c) (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Confidential Settlement Agreements, claimant-identity-shielding option (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1001)
  "This section does not prohibit the entry or enforcement of a provision in any agreement that precludes the disclosure of the amount paid in settlement of a claim."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001(e) (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Confidential Settlement Agreements, settlement-amount confidentiality carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1001)
  Known gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section as the previous clause (nondisparagement_ccp_1001_scope) — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001(c) and (e) — so they are treated as one source with that clause, not independent corroboration of each other or of it. The identity-shielding carve-out is the claimant's option to invoke, not the other side's to impose; nothing in this subsection lets an employer or defendant demand that the claimant's identity be hidden. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.

CALIFORNIA'S BROADER BAN ON SILENCING WORKPLACE-UNLAWFUL-ACTS DISCLOSURES
A separate California statute reaches beyond litigated settlements to ordinary employment and separation agreements generally. It is an unlawful employment practice for an employer to require an employee, as a condition of employment, continued employment, a raise, or a bonus, to sign a nondisparagement agreement or other document to the extent it has the purpose or effect of denying the employee the right to disclose information about unlawful acts in the workplace — defined to include, but not be limited to, information about harassment, discrimination, or any other conduct the employee has reasonable cause to believe is unlawful. The same rule separately applies to any agreement related to an employee's separation from employment: it's an unlawful employment practice for an employer or former employer to include a provision there that prohibits disclosing information about unlawful acts in the workplace. Any nondisparagement or other contractual provision restricting an employee's ability to disclose information about workplace conditions must include specific statutory notice language, in substantial form: "Nothing in this agreement prevents you from discussing or disclosing information about unlawful acts in the workplace, such as harassment or discrimination or any other conduct that you have reason to believe is unlawful." A provision that violates this rule is against public policy and unenforceable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It is an unlawful employment practice for an employer, in exchange for a raise or bonus, or as a condition of employment or continued employment, to do either of the following: ... For an employer to require an employee to sign a nondisparagement agreement or other document to the extent it has the purpose or effect of denying the employee the right to disclose information about unlawful acts in the workplace"
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12964.5(a)(1) (Leginfo text), California Government Code, unlawful employment practice to condition employment on a disclosure-restricting nondisparagement agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12964.5)
  "It is an unlawful employment practice for an employer or former employer to include in any agreement related to an employee’s separation from employment any provision that prohibits the disclosure of information about unlawful acts in the workplace."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12964.5(b)(1) (Leginfo text), California Government Code, unlawful employment practice to include a disclosure-restricting provision in a separation agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12964.5)
  "A nondisparagement or other contractual provision that restricts an employee’s ability to disclose information related to conditions in the workplace shall include, in substantial form, the following language: “Nothing in this agreement prevents you from discussing or disclosing information about unlawful acts in the workplace, such as harassment or discrimination or any other conduct that you have reason to believe is unlawful.”"
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12964.5(a)(1)(B)(ii), (c) (Leginfo text), California Government Code, required notice language and definition of “information about unlawful acts in the workplace” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12964.5)
  Known gap: All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Gov't Code § 12964.5 — (a)(1), (b)(1), and the shared notice-language requirement in (a)(1)(B)/(b)(1)(B) — so they are treated as one source, not independent corroboration of each other. Separately, this statute's own 5-business-day attorney-consultation requirement for a separation agreement (subdivision (b)(4), not quoted here) is a distinct, narrower notice period from the OWBPA's 21/45-day consideration periods for age-discrimination releases covered elsewhere in this corpus's severance-agreement document — the two periods arise under different statutes, serve different purposes, and don't substitute for each other where both independently apply to the same agreement. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.

CARVE-OUTS AND BOUNDARIES OF THE BROADER CALIFORNIA RULE
This broader rule has stated limits. It doesn't apply to a negotiated settlement agreement resolving an underlying claim that has already been filed in court, before an administrative agency, in alternative dispute resolution, or through an employer's internal complaint process — "negotiated" there means voluntary, deliberate, and informed, with consideration of value to the employee and notice of the opportunity to retain an attorney. It does not prohibit a provision that keeps confidential the amount paid in a severance agreement. And it does not stop an employer from protecting its trade secrets, proprietary information, or confidential information that doesn't involve unlawful acts in the workplace. Where a covered separation agreement is offered, the employer must also notify the employee of the right to consult an attorney about it and give at least five business days to do so, though the employee may sign sooner if that shortening is knowing and voluntary and not induced by fraud, misrepresentation, or a threat to withdraw or alter the offer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This section does not apply to a negotiated settlement agreement to resolve an underlying claim under this part that has been filed by an employee in court, before an administrative agency, in an alternative dispute resolution forum, or through an employer’s internal complaint process."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12964.5(d) (Leginfo text), California Government Code, negotiated-settlement-of-a-filed-claim carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12964.5)
  "This section does not prohibit the entry or enforcement of a provision in any agreement that precludes the disclosure of the amount paid in a severance agreement. ... This section does not prohibit an employer from protecting the employer’s trade secrets, proprietary information, or confidential information that does not involve unlawful acts in the workplace."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12964.5(e), (f) (Leginfo text), California Government Code, severance-amount confidentiality and trade-secret/confidential-information carve-outs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12964.5)
  "An employer offering an employee or former employee an agreement related to that employee’s separation from employment as provided in this subdivision shall notify the employee that the employee has a right to consult an attorney regarding the agreement and shall provide the employee with a reasonable time period of not less than five business days in which to do so."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12964.5(b)(4) (Leginfo text), California Government Code, attorney-consultation notice requirement for a covered separation agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12964.5)
  Known gap: All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section as the previous clause (nondisparagement_gov_12964_5_prohibition) — Cal. Gov't Code § 12964.5(d), (e), (f), and (b)(4) — so they are treated as one source with it, not independent corroboration. The negotiated-settlement carve-out in subdivision (d) is what keeps this statute from duplicating or conflicting with the separate settlement-specific statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001) covered earlier in this document: an already-filed claim resolved by a negotiated settlement falls under § 1001's own, narrower rule instead of this one, rather than under both at once. The five-business-day consultation period in (b)(4) applies to a covered separation agreement regardless of the employee's age; it is a different notice period, arising under a different statute, from the OWBPA's 21- or 45-day consideration periods for a valid age-discrimination release. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.

FEDERAL LABOR LAW: SECTION 7 RIGHTS AND SEVERANCE NON-DISPARAGEMENT CLAUSES
Separately from California law, federal law gives most private-sector employees — unionized or not — the right to engage in concerted activity for mutual aid or protection, including discussing wages, working conditions, and workplace disputes with coworkers, a union, government agencies, or others. It's a federal unfair labor practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in exercising that right. Applying these provisions, the National Labor Relations Board held in McLaren Macomb (372 NLRB No. 58, Feb. 21, 2023) that an employer commits an unfair labor practice merely by offering — not just by enforcing — a severance agreement to a covered employee that contains an overly broad non-disparagement or confidentiality provision, where that provision could reasonably be read to restrict the employee's ability to discuss workplace conditions or disputes with coworkers, a union, the Board, another government agency, the media, or others, as part of protected concerted activity. Under this reasoning, the proffer itself can be unlawful even if the employee never signs the agreement and the clause is never invoked.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Employees shall have the right to self-organization, to form, join, or assist labor organizations, to bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing, and to engage in other concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 157 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, National Labor Relations Act, Section 7 — right to engage in concerted activity for mutual aid or protection (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/157)
  "It shall be an unfair labor practice for an employer— (1) to interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in the exercise of the rights guaranteed in section 157 of this title;"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 158(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, National Labor Relations Act, Section 8(a)(1) — unfair labor practice to interfere with Section 7 rights (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/158)
  Known gap: Sourcing honesty note: the McLaren Macomb decision itself was not independently read or quote-verified against primary NLRB text in this research session. CourtListener's case-law search was already rate-limited (125 requests/day, exhausted) before this clause could be checked there, and every attempted direct fetch of nlrb.gov (where NLRB decisions are published) was blocked by this environment's network egress controls. The case's citation, date, and holding as described above are drawn from secondary reporting collected through web search (law-firm client alerts from Holland & Knight, White & Case, Littler, Mintz, and others describing the decision), not from an independently read primary opinion — for that reason, no quotation from the McLaren Macomb opinion itself appears in the citations below; only the two directly fetched and byte-identical-confirmed federal statutory sections are quoted. The same secondary reporting indicates McLaren Macomb remains Board precedent as of mid-2026 (reporting describes an NLRB administrative law judge applying it in a May 2026 case, Detrex Corporation) even though the NLRB General Counsel's own explanatory guidance on it (Memorandum GC 23-05) was rescinded by an Acting General Counsel in February 2025 — a General Counsel memo is prosecutorial guidance, not binding Board law, so its rescission doesn't by itself overrule the underlying decision, but this document's account of that rescission and its practical significance also rests on the same secondary sourcing, not on an independently read primary NLRB document. Both statutory citations below are drawn from separate, independently numbered sections (29 U.S.C. §§ 157 and 158), not subsections of one section. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the employer or employee is in — unlike the California statutes elsewhere in this document — but whether it protects a specific person's specific statement still turns on facts this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is lawful or enforceable in a specific case.

WHO SECTION 7 DOESN'T COVER: THE SUPERVISOR EXCLUSION
The federal protection above is not universal. The National Labor Relations Act's own definition of "employee" — the term Section 7's rights are written around — expressly excludes several categories of workers, including any individual employed as a supervisor, along with independent contractors, agricultural laborers, domestic workers in a private home, and certain railway-industry employees. Because Section 7 protection, and the reasoning applied in McLaren Macomb, run to "employees" as the Act defines that term, someone who meets the Act's own definition of "supervisor" generally falls outside that protection.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "shall not include any individual employed as an agricultural laborer, or in the domestic service of any family or person at his home, or any individual employed by his parent or spouse, or any individual having the status of an independent contractor, or any individual employed as a supervisor, or any individual employed by an employer subject to the Railway Labor Act"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 152(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, National Labor Relations Act, definition of “employee” and the supervisor exclusion (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/152)
  Known gap: "Supervisor" is itself a separately defined term under the same statute (29 U.S.C. § 152(11), not independently fetched or quoted for this clause), generally turning on whether a person has authority to hire, fire, discipline, or responsibly direct other employees using independent judgment — not simply on having a manager-sounding job title. Whether a specific employee meets that definition is a fact-specific question this document doesn't resolve. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 152(3)); no additional independent source was found for this beyond that subsection. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the employer or employee is in — unlike the California statutes elsewhere in this document — but whether it protects a specific person's specific statement still turns on facts this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is lawful or enforceable in a specific case.

NON-DISPARAGEMENT CLAUSES AS ORDINARY CONTRACT TERMS
Outside the specific statutory contexts above, California has no single statute that bans non-disparagement clauses generally — unlike, for example, its broad statutory restriction on employee noncompete agreements. A non-disparagement clause outside those specific contexts is ordinarily treated as just another contract term, subject to the same general rules that apply to any contract provision under California law: a term is not lawful if it is contrary to an express provision of law, contrary to the policy of the law even without an express prohibition, or otherwise contrary to good morals, and a contract term that tries to exempt someone from responsibility for their own fraud, willful injury to another, or violation of law is against the policy of the law. Within that framework, a non-disparagement clause that doesn't run into one of the specific statutory bans described elsewhere in this document is generally enforced like any other bargained-for contract restriction.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "That is not lawful which is: 1. Contrary to an express provision of law; 2. Contrary to the policy of express law, though not expressly prohibited; or, 3. Otherwise contrary to good morals."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1667 (Leginfo text), California Civil Code, general definition of an unlawful contract term (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1667.)
  "All contracts which have for their object, directly or indirectly, to exempt any one from responsibility for his own fraud, or willful injury to the person or property of another, or violation of law, whether willful or negligent, are against the policy of the law."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1668 (Leginfo text), California Civil Code, contract terms exempting a party from responsibility for fraud or violation of law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1668.)
  Known gap: § 1667 and § 1668 are two separate, independently numbered statutory sections, not subsections of one section. These are old, general-purpose statutes (both enacted in 1872) applied here to a modern contract type; no case law applying them specifically to a non-disparagement clause was checked in this research, so this clause states the general statutory backdrop rather than a case-tested application of it to this particular kind of provision. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.

NON-DISPARAGEMENT VS. CONFIDENTIALITY, AND WHETHER TRUTH IS A DEFENSE
A non-disparagement clause and a confidentiality (nondisclosure) clause are often drafted together in a single paragraph and colloquially treated as interchangeable, but they restrict different things. A confidentiality clause restricts disclosing information at all, regardless of whether the information is flattering, neutral, or damaging. A non-disparagement clause instead restricts making negative or critical statements — it doesn't stop someone from disclosing information so much as from characterizing it unfavorably. California's own statute in this area draws that same distinction in its own text, separately regulating a provision that "prevents or restricts the disclosure of factual information" and a provision precluding disclosure of a settlement amount, rather than treating all restrictions on speech about a claim as one undifferentiated category. Whether a truthful statement can still count as "disparaging" for purposes of a contract's own non-disparagement clause is a genuinely open question as a matter of ordinary contract interpretation: a non-disparagement clause's own wording may or may not include a truth-based defense, and courts interpreting a given clause look to what that specific clause's language actually says, not to a single fixed legal rule that truth is always, or never, an excuse.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "a provision within a settlement agreement that prevents or restricts the disclosure of factual information related to a claim filed in a civil action or a complaint filed in an administrative action"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001(a) (Leginfo text), California Code of Civil Procedure, Confidential Settlement Agreements, disclosure of factual information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1001)
  Known gap: The first citation below is the same statutory section as nondisparagement_ccp_1001_scope and nondisparagement_ccp_1001_carveouts (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001) — it is not independent corroboration of those clauses, and is used here only as evidence that the fact/opinion distinction described above has a real textual hook in California statute, not as a general rule that all non-disparagement clauses everywhere draw that same line. The point about truthful statements possibly still being "disparaging" is stated honestly as an open, unresolved question rather than settled either way — no single California or federal statute was found in this research that resolves it as a general matter, and this document does not resolve it either. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.

MUTUAL NON-DISPARAGEMENT
Acme Corp and Jordan Alex Lee mutually agree not to make any statement, written or oral, that disparages the other, including (for Jordan Alex Lee) Acme Corp's officers, directors, and management-level employees acting in that capacity, and (for Acme Corp) Jordan Alex Lee. This does not restrict either party from: providing truthful information in response to a subpoena, court order, or valid request from a government agency; filing a charge or complaint with, or participating in an investigation or proceeding conducted by, a government agency; discussing or disclosing information about unlawful acts in the workplace, including harassment, discrimination, or any other conduct either party has reason to believe is unlawful; or making truthful statements in a legal proceeding between the parties. Nothing in this clause limits any right either party has under federal labor law to discuss wages, hours, or other terms and conditions of employment.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate agreement to the terms above.

Acme Corp
By: _______________
Name/Title: _______________
Date: October 15, 2026

Employee: Jordan Alex Lee
Signature: _______________
Date: October 15, 2026

expectedJSON.body: A separate California statute reaches beyond litigated settlements to ordinary employment and separation agreements generally. It is an unlawful employment practice for an employer to require an employee, as a condition of employment, continued employment, a raise, or a bonus, to sign a nondisparagement agreement or other document to the extent it has the purpose or effect of denying the employee the right to disclose information about unlawful acts in the workplace — defined to include, but not be limited to, information about harassment, discrimination, or any other conduct the employee has reasonable cause to believe is unlawful. The same rule separately applies to any agreement related to an employee's separation from employment: it's an unlawful employment practice for an employer or former employer to include a provision there that prohibits disclosing information about unlawful acts in the workplace. Any nondisparagement or other contractual provision restricting an employee's ability to disclose information about workplace conditions must include specific statutory notice language, in substantial form: "Nothing in this agreement prevents you from discussing or disclosing information about unlawful acts in the workplace, such as harassment or discrimination or any other conduct that you have reason to believe is unlawful." A provision that violates this rule is against public policy and unenforceable.

expectedJSON.body: This broader rule has stated limits. It doesn't apply to a negotiated settlement agreement resolving an underlying claim that has already been filed in court, before an administrative agency, in alternative dispute resolution, or through an employer's internal complaint process — "negotiated" there means voluntary, deliberate, and informed, with consideration of value to the employee and notice of the opportunity to retain an attorney. It does not prohibit a provision that keeps confidential the amount paid in a severance agreement. And it does not stop an employer from protecting its trade secrets, proprietary information, or confidential information that doesn't involve unlawful acts in the workplace. Where a covered separation agreement is offered, the employer must also notify the employee of the right to consult an attorney about it and give at least five business days to do so, though the employee may sign sooner if that shortening is knowing and voluntary and not induced by fraud, misrepresentation, or a threat to withdraw or alter the offer.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from California law, federal law gives most private-sector employees — unionized or not — the right to engage in concerted activity for mutual aid or protection, including discussing wages, working conditions, and workplace disputes with coworkers, a union, government agencies, or others. It's a federal unfair labor practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in exercising that right. Applying these provisions, the National Labor Relations Board held in McLaren Macomb (372 NLRB No. 58, Feb. 21, 2023) that an employer commits an unfair labor practice merely by offering — not just by enforcing — a severance agreement to a covered employee that contains an overly broad non-disparagement or confidentiality provision, where that provision could reasonably be read to restrict the employee's ability to discuss workplace conditions or disputes with coworkers, a union, the Board, another government agency, the media, or others, as part of protected concerted activity. Under this reasoning, the proffer itself can be unlawful even if the employee never signs the agreement and the clause is never invoked.

citations.quote: Employees shall have the right to self-organization, to form, join, or assist labor organizations, to bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing, and to engage in other concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection

expectedJSON.body: The federal protection above is not universal. The National Labor Relations Act's own definition of "employee" — the term Section 7's rights are written around — expressly excludes several categories of workers, including any individual employed as a supervisor, along with independent contractors, agricultural laborers, domestic workers in a private home, and certain railway-industry employees. Because Section 7 protection, and the reasoning applied in McLaren Macomb, run to "employees" as the Act defines that term, someone who meets the Act's own definition of "supervisor" generally falls outside that protection.

expectedJSON.body: Outside the specific statutory contexts above, California has no single statute that bans non-disparagement clauses generally — unlike, for example, its broad statutory restriction on employee noncompete agreements. A non-disparagement clause outside those specific contexts is ordinarily treated as just another contract term, subject to the same general rules that apply to any contract provision under California law: a term is not lawful if it is contrary to an express provision of law, contrary to the policy of the law even without an express prohibition, or otherwise contrary to good morals, and a contract term that tries to exempt someone from responsibility for their own fraud, willful injury to another, or violation of law is against the policy of the law. Within that framework, a non-disparagement clause that doesn't run into one of the specific statutory bans described elsewhere in this document is generally enforced like any other bargained-for contract restriction.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, general definition of an unlawful contract term
citations.quote: That is not lawful which is: 1. Contrary to an express provision of law; 2. Contrary to the policy of express law, though not expressly prohibited; or, 3. Otherwise contrary to good morals.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, contract terms exempting a party from responsibility for fraud or violation of law
citations.quote: All contracts which have for their object, directly or indirectly, to exempt any one from responsibility for his own fraud, or willful injury to the person or property of another, or violation of law, whether willful or negligent, are against the policy of the law.

expectedJSON.body: A non-disparagement clause and a confidentiality (nondisclosure) clause are often drafted together in a single paragraph and colloquially treated as interchangeable, but they restrict different things. A confidentiality clause restricts disclosing information at all, regardless of whether the information is flattering, neutral, or damaging. A non-disparagement clause instead restricts making negative or critical statements — it doesn't stop someone from disclosing information so much as from characterizing it unfavorably. California's own statute in this area draws that same distinction in its own text, separately regulating a provision that "prevents or restricts the disclosure of factual information" and a provision precluding disclosure of a settlement amount, rather than treating all restrictions on speech about a claim as one undifferentiated category. Whether a truthful statement can still count as "disparaging" for purposes of a contract's own non-disparagement clause is a genuinely open question as a matter of ordinary contract interpretation: a non-disparagement clause's own wording may or may not include a truth-based defense, and courts interpreting a given clause look to what that specific clause's language actually says, not to a single fixed legal rule that truth is always, or never, an excuse.

citations.quote: a provision within a settlement agreement that prevents or restricts the disclosure of factual information related to a claim filed in a civil action or a complaint filed in an administrative action
